name: Son Clave 3-2
desc: The foundational five-stroke son clave with the three-side first; the third stroke of the three-side falls on the 'and' of beat 2. It is the rhythmic key of son, salsa and most Cuban dance music.

name: Son Clave 2-3
desc: Son clave with the two-side leading; the same key as 3-2 but rotated so the cycle begins on the off-beat two-side. Common in many salsa arrangements that start 2-3.

name: Rumba Clave 3-2
desc: The rumba clave (3-2) differs from son clave by delaying the third stroke of the three-side by one sixteenth, landing on the 'a' of beat 2. It is the key pattern of guaguancó and yambú.

name: Rumba Clave 2-3
desc: Rumba clave with the two-side first; the rotated form of the rumba key used when a rumba phrase begins on the two-side.

name: 6/8 Afro-Cuban Clave (3-2)
desc: The triple-pulse Afro-Cuban clave underlying 6/8 toques; its six strokes derive from the standard bell and align with rumba columbia and bembé. Notated here in a 12-pulse cycle (snareAccent maps to the 6/8 clave attacks).

name: 6/8 Standard Bell (Bembé)
desc: The seven-stroke standard pattern (ethnomusicology's 'standard bell'), played on hoe-blade or agogo in Cuban bembé and 6/8 folkloric music. It is the master timeline for triple-pulse Afro-Cuban styles.

name: 6/8 Bell 2-3
desc: The standard 6/8 bell rotated to begin on its two-side, the alternate orientation of the bembé timeline used when the song phrase leads with the weaker half.

name: Cáscara 2-3 Son
desc: Cáscara ('shell') played on the side of the timbales, derived from rumba palitos; this 2-3 son orientation interlocks with son clave and drives the timbal groove in salsa.

name: Cáscara 3-2 Son
desc: The 3-2 orientation of the timbal cáscara/shell pattern; its accents trace the three-side then two-side of son clave and outline the salsa pulse on the timbale shell.

name: Son Montuno
desc: The driving son montuno feel with an anticipated-bass tumbao (bombardeo) playing the 'and-of-2' and 'and-of-4' over son clave 3-2. It is the engine of son cubano and modern salsa.

name: Conga Tumbao (Marcha)
desc: The basic conga tumbao (marcha): open tones on the 'and' of beats 2 and 4 with heel-toe filler, the standard accompaniment in son and salsa. Bass holds the open tones; clave shown in snareAccent.

name: Changüí
desc: Changüí from Guantánamo, ancestor of son, built on interlocking marímbula bass and bongó-del-monte; its syncopated swing predates fixed clave. Here the bongó/guayo accents sit in snareAccent and marímbula in bass.

name: Nengón
desc: Nengón, the rural eastern Cuban proto-son from which changüí descends, with a simple call-and-response tres ostinato over marímbula bass. One of the oldest documented Cuban son roots.

name: Kiribá
desc: Kiribá, a Baracoa-region relative of nengón and changüí, an archaic eastern son form with cyclic tres and marímbula interplay. Part of the changüí complex of Guantánamo.

name: Danzón (Baqueteo)
desc: The baqueteo of danzón, played on güiro and timbal heads, built on the cinquillo cell (the 3-side cinquillo, then the 2-side). It is the genteel charanga rhythm derived from the contradanza.

name: Cinquillo Cell
desc: The cinquillo, a five-stroke Afro-Cuban/Haitian rhythmic cell underpinning danzón, contradanza and bolero; two cinquillo cells per measure here outline its characteristic long-short pulse.

name: Cha-cha-chá
desc: Cha-cha-chá, created by Enrique Jorrín, marked by the timbal cowbell on every quarter and the güiro's 'cha-cha-chá' triplet feel on beats 4-and-1. A charanga dance derived from the danzón-mambo.

name: Mambo
desc: Mambo, the up-tempo big-band offshoot of the danzón-mambo and son, with the mambo bell playing constant eighths (crescendo per group of four) over an anticipated bass tumbao.

name: Guajira
desc: Guajira, the lyrical countryside son derived from the punto guajiro, set over son clave 3-2 with a gentle anticipated bass. Associated with Guantanamera and the campesino repertoire.

name: Guaracha
desc: Guaracha, a fast, witty, up-tempo Cuban song-dance form often in 2-3 son clave, a staple of comedic theater and later salsa. Driven by brisk tumbao and cáscara.

name: Bolero (Cuban)
desc: The Cuban bolero, a slow romantic 2/4 ballad built on the cinquillo cell played with bongó and maracas. Distinct from the Spanish bolero, it originated in Santiago de Cuba.

name: Bolero-Son
desc: Bolero-son, the hybrid that fused the slow bolero melody with the son montuno's clave and anticipated bass, the prototype for romantic salsa ballads.

name: Pilón
desc: Pilón, created by Pacho Alonso and Enrique Bonne in the 1960s, evoking the pounding motion of grinding coffee in a mortar (pilón); a syncopated oriente dance over son clave.

name: Mozambique (Pello el Afrokán)
desc: Mozambique, invented by Pello el Afrokán (Pedro Izquierdo) in Havana c.1963 from comparsa and rumba, with massed bombos, hoe-blades and cowbells in a 3-2 conga feel.

name: Mozambique (NY/Palmieri)
desc: The New York Mozambique codified by Eddie Palmieri and Manny Oquendo, where a guaguancó-derived cáscara bell over 2-3 clave drives the groove with bombo and clave on the heads.

name: Conga de Comparsa (Havana)
desc: Havana-style conga de comparsa (carnival), with bombo on the downbeats and a campana/sartén bell pattern related to the cáscara, propelling the marching comparsa.

name: Conga de Comparsa (Santiago)
desc: Santiago de Cuba conga (conga santiaguera/conga oriental), faster and busier than the Havana style, featuring the corneta china and a dense battery of bells, bocú and quinto.

name: Songo
desc: Songo, developed by Changuito (José Luis Quintana) with Los Van Van, the first Cuban popular rhythm to fuse rumba and funk on a drumset/timbal hybrid over son clave.

name: Timba
desc: Timba, the aggressive 1990s evolution of songo (NG La Banda, Los Van Van), layering rumba, funk and jazz over a dense rumba-clave-aligned groove with broken anticipated bass.

name: Rumba Yambú
desc: Yambú, the slow, old-style rumba ('rumba de cajón') danced gently by couples without the vacunao, set on rumba clave with cajones or congas. The most stately of the rumba styles.

name: Rumba Guaguancó
desc: Guaguancó, the most popular medium-tempo rumba, organized by rumba clave with salidor (tumba), tres-dos (segundo) and quinto leading the flirtatious vacunao dance.

name: Guaguancó Palitos (Guagua)
desc: The palitos/guagua (catá) part of guaguancó, sticks striking a hollow bamboo to lay down the cáscara-like timeline that interlocks with rumba clave. This bell-line is the ancestor of salsa cáscara.

name: Rumba Columbia (6/8)
desc: Columbia, the fast, virtuosic, male solo rumba in 6/8 with strong Abakuá and Congo influence, organized by the standard bell over 6/8 clave. The most acrobatic rumba style.

name: Guarapachangueo
desc: Guarapachangueo, the modern Havana rumba style created by Los Chinitos, highly conversational with cajón/box bass and a fluid interplay of beats and rests over rumba clave.

name: Batá-Rumba
desc: Batá-rumba, created by AfroCuba de Matanzas, fusing batá toques (chachalokafún) with guaguancó so consecrated drums converse with the rumba quinto over rumba clave.

name: Bembé
desc: Bembé, a festive Afro-Cuban religious drumming celebration in 6/8 using the standard bell (played on hoe-blade) with shekere and tumbadoras. A semi-secular gathering honoring the orichas.

name: Iyesá
desc: Iyesá, a sacred Lucumí drum-and-bell tradition from the Ilesha (Yoruba) people, played on four cylindrical iyesá drums and agogo in duple meter for orichas like Ochún and Ogún.

name: Palo (Congo)
desc: Palo, the Bantu/Congo-derived sacred drumming of the Reglas de Congo (Palo Monte), with ngoma drums and guagua bell in a driving duple groove for the nkisi spirits.

name: Yuka
desc: Yuka, a secular Congo dance and drumming from Pinar del Río using three wooden yuka drums (caja, mula, cachimbo) with a guagua/reja bell, ancestor of the makuta and rumba.

name: Makuta
desc: Makuta, a Congo-derived fertility dance and drumming in which the cinquillo is sounded on the bell (Havana style); a Bantu ancestral root of Cuban rumba and conga.

name: Abakuá
desc: Abakuá (Ñáñigo), the secret Cross River (Ekpe/Efik) male-society drumming with the ekón bell and bonkó drums; its triplet-tinged 4/4 feel is a deep root of rumba columbia.

name: Abakuá (6/8)
desc: The triple-pulse Abakuá timeline played on the ekón, sharing the standard 6/8 bell; this ritual feel directly underlies rumba columbia's Abakuá-derived phrasing.

name: Batá: Latopa (Oru Seco opening)
desc: Latopa, the opening salute of the oru seco played by the three batá (iyá, itótele, okónkolo) to greet Elegguá; an interlocking 4/4 invocation that begins the drum liturgy.

name: Batá: Chachalokafún (Obatalá)
desc: Chachalokafún (chachalokuá), a fundamental 4/4 batá toque associated with Obatalá and used widely across the liturgy; the okónkolo holds a steady timeline while iyá and itótele converse.

name: Batá: Toque to Elegguá
desc: A 6/8 batá toque saluting Elegguá, the trickster gatekeeper oricha who opens and closes the paths; played first so the ceremony may proceed. Triple-pulse okónkolo timeline.

name: Batá: Toque to Ogún
desc: A 6/8 batá toque for Ogún, the warrior oricha of iron and labor; its martial, driving triple-pulse phrasing summons the orisha of the machete and forge.

name: Batá: Toque to Yemayá
desc: A flowing 6/8 batá toque for Yemayá, oricha of the sea and motherhood; its rolling triple-pulse feel evokes ocean waves and is among the most beloved salutes.

name: Batá: Toque to Changó (Aluyá)
desc: Aluyá, a fast, fiery 6/8 batá toque for Changó, oricha of thunder, fire and drumming; its driving triple pulse accompanies the most energetic Changó dances.

name: Batá: Toque to Oyá
desc: A 6/8 batá toque for Oyá, oricha of wind, lightning, storms and the cemetery gates; its gusting triple-pulse phrasing mirrors her tempestuous nature.

name: Batá: Toque to Ochún
desc: A 6/8 batá toque for Ochún, oricha of rivers, love and sweetness; its lilting triple-pulse phrasing accompanies her graceful, flirtatious dance.

name: Batá: Toque to Obatalá
desc: A stately 4/4 batá toque for Obatalá, the calm white-clad oricha of creation, purity and wisdom; played slowly and majestically to honor the father of the orichas.

name: Batá: Toque to Babalú-Ayé
desc: A batá toque for Babalú-Ayé (San Lázaro), oricha of disease and healing; a measured, limping 4/4 feel reflecting the orisha who walks with crutches.

name: Batá: Oru Seco Nyongo
desc: Nyongo (ñongo), a versatile 6/8 batá toque from the oru seco used to accompany many orichas; one of the most common chant-rhythms in the toque de santo.

name: Songo (6/8 variant)
desc: A 6/8 songo feel that Changuito and Los Van Van wove from Afro-Cuban folkloric 6/8 toques into the popular drumset/timbal vocabulary, bridging bembé and dance music.

name: Son (2-3) Tumbao
desc: The classic son cubano groove in 2-3 son clave, with the anticipated bass (bajo anticipado) playing the 'and-of-2' and 'and-of-4'. The blueprint of the son sextet and salsa rhythm section.

name: Bongó Martillo
desc: Martillo ('hammer'), the steady bongó pattern of son and salsa, marking continuous eighths with an accented open tone (macho) on beat 4. The bongocero's foundational groove.

name: Conga de Comparsa Bell (Campana)
desc: The campana/sartén bell line of the Havana conga de comparsa, a syncopated steel-pan timeline that locks with the bombo and propels the carnival comparsa forward.

name: Pachanga
desc: Pachanga, a fast, bouncy charanga dance craze of the late 1950s-60s blending son montuno and merengue, marked by its lively syncopated güiro and timbal feel.

name: Mambo Bell (Bongó Campana)
desc: The bongó campana (hand cowbell) part used in the mambo/montuno section, playing steady eighths with accents on the downbeats and 'ands' to lift the salsa chorus.
